concept.technique_name: counting terms of an arithmetic progression

examples.problem_statement: At Goli-Vadapav, an automatic machine makes vadapavs at 1 vadapav per half a minute, adding fillings as follows: the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, ... vadapavs get a chicken patty; the 1st, 5th, 9th, ... get a vegetable patty; the 1st, 8th, 17th, ... get a mushroom patty; and the rest get plain cheese and tomato fillings. The machine makes exactly 500 vadapavs per day. How many vadapavs per day are made with cheese and tomato as fillings?

solution.description: Start from the daily output stated in the data: the machine makes exactly 500 vadapavs per day, which is the pool every filling is carved out of.
Count the terms of the odd-numbered chicken-patty series up to 499; that count, 250, is how many vadapavs are chicken-filled and therefore not plain.
Count the terms of the series 8, 22, 36, ... to get the 36 vadapavs that take a mushroom patty without already being counted among the chicken ones.
Subtract both filled groups from the daily total, leaving the vadapavs that received no patty at all and so got cheese and tomato.

key_reminders: The number of terms in an arithmetic series a, a+d, ..., L is (L-a)/d + 1.
Vadapavs that receive no patty from any of the listed series are exactly the ones with cheese and tomato.
Groups must be counted without double counting: only the mushroom vadapavs not already counted as chicken are subtracted.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the full mushroom series count instead of only the mushroom-only count, double counting positions that are already odd-numbered.
Treating the vegetable-patty series (1, 5, 9, ...) as a separate subtraction, though every one of its terms is odd and already inside the chicken count.

examples.problem_statement: Study the following table of loans disbursed by 5 banks (Rupees in Crores) and answer the question below. Bank A: 1982 = 18, 1983 = 23, 1984 = 45, 1985 = 30, 1986 = 70. Bank B: 27, 33, 18, 41, 37. Bank C: 29, 29, 22, 17, 11. Bank D: 31, 16, 28, 32, 43. Bank E: 13, 19, 27, 34, 42. Total: 118, 120, 140, 154, 203. In which of the following banks did the disbursement of loans continuously increase over the years?

solution.description: Pull out the five yearly figures for bank E from the table so the year-on-year movement can be read off in one line.

solution.result: every year is higher than the one before it
solution.description: Compare each figure with the one to its left; each comparison holds, so the row rises without a single dip.

solution.operation: \text{match the continuously rising row to its option}
solution.description: Since E is the row whose values rise at every step, pick the answer choice naming bank E.

key_reminders: "Continuously increase" requires every consecutive year to be higher, not just the last year above the first.
A single dip anywhere in a row disqualifies that bank.
common_mistakes: Choosing bank A because it ends far higher (18 to 70) while ignoring the drop from 45 in 1984 to 30 in 1985.
Choosing bank D on its overall rise while ignoring the fall from 31 to 16 between 1982 and 1983.

concept.technique_name: vertical angles and angles on a straight line

examples.problem_statement: In the figure, angles b, c, and d lie along a straight line, and angles c and f are vertical angles. If c + f = 70, and d = 80, what is b?

solution.result: c and f have equal measure
solution.description: Recognise that c and f are vertical angles, which lets you treat their two measures as one unknown.
Replace f by c in the given sum and halve it, giving the individual measure of each of the two equal angles.
Write the straight-line relation for b, c, and d, then substitute the value of c just found and the given d.
Solve the straight-line equation for b by subtracting the two known angle measures from 180.

key_reminders: Vertical angles are equal in measure.
Angles that together form a straight line sum to 180 degrees.
common_mistakes: Using 70 directly as c instead of splitting the given sum of the two equal vertical angles into 35 each.
Setting b + c + d equal to 90 or 360 rather than the 180 degrees of a straight line.

concept.technique_name: testing answer choices for full determination in a hybrid ordering-grouping game

examples.problem_statement: A photographer will take three photographs of a high school math team. The seven members of the team - P, R, S, T, V, W, and X - will each appear in exactly one of the photographs. There will be exactly one member in the first photograph, three members in the second photograph, and three members in the third photograph. The following conditions apply: P does not appear in a later photo than does T or X. R and S will appear in the same photograph together. V and X will not be photographed together. Which of the following pairs of assignments would determine the team members for each photograph?

solution.operation: \text{list what the correct answer must settle: place the RS chunk, arrange P, T, X, and keep V apart from X}
solution.result: three jobs the winning pair of assignments has to finish
solution.description: Before testing choices, note everything that must be pinned down, so a choice that leaves any of these open can be dropped fast.

solution.operation: \text{(A) V in Photo 1, R in Photo 2}
solution.description: This fixes V and the chunk, and forces T and X into group 3 since neither may precede P; but groups 2 and 3 each keep one open slot that W or P could fill either way.

solution.operation: \text{(B) V in Photo 1, R in Photo 3}
solution.description: This forces P into group 2, yet group 3's remaining place could still go to T, X, or W, leaving the arrangement even less settled than (A).

solution.operation: \text{(C) P in Photo 1, R in Photo 2}
solution.description: This locks in P and the chunk and, by requiring V and X to be split between groups 2 and 3, forces T and W into group 3; but V and X remain interchangeable.

solution.operation: \text{(D) P in Photo 1, V in Photo 3}
solution.description: This places P, X, and V in groups 1, 2, and 3, but nothing here says where the RS chunk goes, so the photographs are not settled.

solution.operation: \text{(E) W in Photo 1, R in Photo 2} \Rightarrow X \text{ barred from group 2}
solution.result: V in group 2; P, T, X form group 3 - fully determined
solution.description: This locks the chunk into group 2 with W alone in group 1; since X cannot come before P it cannot take group 2's last slot, so V goes there and P, T, and X fill group 3, settling every photograph.

key_reminders: R and S must occupy the same photograph, so they move as a single two-person chunk.
P may not appear later than T or X, which bars X from any group ahead of P.
V and X can never share a photograph, so they must be split across the two three-member groups.
common_mistakes: Accepting a choice like (A) or (C) that fixes most placements while two members stay interchangeable, since "determine" demands a single complete arrangement.
Forgetting to apply the P-before-X restriction when filling the last open slot in group 2, which is exactly what settles choice (E).
